section: Educational Psychology · Ch1 — Domains of Development (Complete)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A five-year-old can now button their own shirt, hop on one foot, and hold a pencil with good control — improvements in fine and gross muscle coordination. These changes belong to which domain of development?
explanation: The physical-motor domain covers bodily growth and the development of gross motor skills (hopping, running) and fine motor skills (buttoning, pencil grip) — distinct from cognitive (thinking), language, or social-emotional domains.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch1 — Domains of Development (Complete)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A two-year-old's vocabulary rapidly expands from around 50 words to combining two-word phrases like 'more milk' and 'go park'. This rapid growth in expressive and receptive vocabulary belongs to which domain of development?
explanation: The language domain covers the development of vocabulary, grammar, and communication ability — the described vocabulary explosion and two-word combining ('telegraphic speech') is a hallmark milestone of this domain around age two.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch1 — Domains of Development (Complete)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A child with a physical-motor delay affecting speech-muscle coordination may also show slower vocabulary development, illustrating that the domains of development (physical, cognitive, language, social-emotional) are:

options.option_text: Interrelated and mutually influential, not entirely independent of one another
Completely independent, with zero influence on each other
Identical to each other, with no real distinction
Relevant only to infants, not older children

explanation: Although the domains are conceptually distinguished for study, real development is holistic — a delay in one domain (physical/motor speech mechanisms) can genuinely affect another (language) — they are interrelated, not siloed.
